---
order: 8
unit: agreement
title: Our class agreement
summary: "A short, teacher-led lesson. The class looks back at the habits from the course, sorts what makes a good agreement (short, positive, about what we do, something everyone can keep), reads a made-up class's draft, and then writes its own agreement together for how it treats each other online."
language: science
shape: 5e
hook: "A made-up Year 6 class wrote 25 rules for being online. Nobody could remember them by Friday. How could they make an agreement people actually keep?"
---
This lesson is mostly a class discussion. Your teacher leads it, and the class writes its agreement together. You do not need to share anything about yourself.

## Engage: rules or agreement?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a guess: a short agreement the class writes is easier to keep than a long list of rules from someone else."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Which is people most likely to keep?"
  options: ["Five short lines the class wrote and agreed together", "25 rules written by someone else", "No agreement at all"]
  actual: "Usually the short one the class wrote. People keep what they helped make and can remember."
```

## Explore: what makes a good line?

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting draft lines shows what a good agreement line looks like: short, positive, about what we do."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Is each draft line a good line for a class agreement, or does it need work?"
  options: ["Good line", "Needs work"]
  items:
    - ["We pause before we post.", "Good line", "Short, positive, and something we do."]
    - ["Never ever do anything bad online or you'll be in big trouble!!!", "Needs work", "It's a threat, and 'anything bad' doesn't say what to do."]
    - ["We ask before we share a photo of someone.", "Good line", "Clear and kind."]
    - ["We tell a trusted adult when something worries us, and we help friends to tell.", "Good line", "It names what to do and who helps."]
    - ["Don't use phones.", "Needs work", "Nobody will keep it, and it isn't about how we treat each other."]
    - ["If someone in our class is having a hard time online, we don't add to it.", "Good line", "It's about what bystanders do."]
```

Was your guess right? Good lines are **short**, **positive** (what we do, not what we don't), and **something everyone can keep**.

## Explain: a made-up class's agreement

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Reading a finished example gives the class a model before writing its own."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Read the made-up class's agreement below. Which course habit is missing from it?"
  options: ["Slowing down when something pushes you to hurry", "Pausing before you post", "Asking before sharing a photo of someone", "Telling a trusted adult"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Line 1 is about pausing.", "Line 2 is about asking first.", "Line 4 is about telling."]
  explain: "Nothing in it is about pressure and tricks. A class could add one, or decide five lines is enough."
```

**Room 12's online agreement** (made up)

1. We pause before we post, and choose the kinder version.
2. We ask before we share a photo or message about someone else.
3. We keep personal details for people we know in real life.
4. We tell a trusted adult when something worries us, and help friends to tell.
5. If someone is having a hard time online, we don't add to it, and we check on them.

Every line came from a lesson in this course. Your class's agreement can look quite different. What matters is that **you write it together** and that **everyone can keep it**.

## Make: our agreement

```step
stage: make
insight: "The class writes and agrees its own lines, led by the teacher; the site holds a tick, not the agreement."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I helped my class write our agreement, and I can say one line from it." }
```

Your teacher will lead this part. In small groups, write one or two lines, then the class chooses and agrees five or so. Use the course's habits if they help:

- **A day's trail:** can I take it back, does it say where I am, is it about someone else?
- **Who can see this?** The smallest audience that does the job.
- **Pause before you post:** how will they read it?
- **Who is on the other end?** Friendly is not the same as known.
- **Screens and me:** notice, then choose.
- **Pressure and tricks:** stop, check, ask.
- **When something goes wrong:** stop, keep it, tell, block and report.

## Evaluate: keep it going

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I know where our class agreement is kept, and who to tell if something goes wrong." }
```

**A private think** (just for you): which line of the agreement will be easiest for you to keep? Which will be hardest?

```teacher
summary: A short, teacher-led lesson that closes the course. Students sort draft
  lines into good lines and lines that need work, read a made-up class's
  five-line agreement, then the class writes and agrees its own. The site holds
  only ticks; the agreement itself is the class's, kept wherever the teacher
  chooses.
time: 40
timing: Engage and Explore 8 min · Explain 5 min · Make (class writing) 20 min ·
  Evaluate 7 min
goals:
  - I can say what makes a good line for an agreement.
  - I can help write our class's agreement.
  - I can say one line from it and who to tell if something goes wrong.
struggle: "Groups write rules for other people ('people shouldn't...') or long
  lists. Ask: what will we do? Can you say it in under ten words?"
before: >
  **⚑ Wellbeing review:** this course is a draft. Share this lesson and these
  notes with the school's wellbeing lead before teaching. Check the agreement
  fits the school's own policies on devices, bullying and reporting, and doesn't
  promise anything the school can't do.


  **If a student discloses something:** follow the school's child-protection
  procedure. Listen, don't probe, don't promise to keep it secret, and pass it
  on as the procedure says. Thank them, and keep the class talk on the
  agreement, not on events.


  **Ground rules:** Room 12 is made up. Don't let lines name or point at real
  people or real events in the class. Keep the agreement positive (what we do)
  rather than a list of bans. The closing think is private.


  **Why this is a lesson, not only a class plan:** it sits in the course order,
  so students and the course page see the course end here; it gets a teacher
  guide and slides like the others; and students can come back to the made-up
  example. The real work, writing the agreement, happens in the room. The site
  stores nothing the class writes.


  Run it: groups of three write one or two lines on paper (10 min); the class
  reads them out, groups similar ones and chooses about five (10 min); write the
  final version on a poster or a shared page the school approves. Revisit it
  after a few weeks.
running:
  - "Engage: ask who remembers any of the school's rules word for word."
  - "Explore: ask what the 'needs work' lines have in common."
  - "Explain: ask which line of Room 12's agreement they'd keep, and which
    they'd change."
  - "Make: groups first, then the whole class. Read lines aloud without saying
    which group wrote them."
  - "Evaluate: say where the agreement will be kept and when you'll look at it
    again."
stuck:
  - see: A group writes a list of don'ts.
    ask: What would we do instead?
    fix: "Turn each don't into a do: 'Don't be mean' becomes 'We choose the kinder
      version'."
  - see: A line points at a real person or event.
    ask: Could anyone in any class keep this line?
    fix: Make it general, and follow up privately if it hints at something real.
  - see: The class can't agree on a line.
    ask: Can everyone keep it?
    fix: Leave it out or reword it; five lines everyone keeps beats ten that some
      don't.
stretch: Write the agreement for a younger class, using words they would understand.
support: "Sentence starters on the board: We pause... We ask... We tell... We help..."
leads: >
  End of the course. Revisit the agreement after a few weeks: which line is
  working, and which needs changing?


  Links: How computers work › Cyber safety and privacy (Years 7 and 8;
  passwords, second factors and phishing in more depth).
exit:
  q: Say one line from our class agreement.
  a: Any line the class agreed.
explain: >
  A good agreement is **short**, **positive** (what we do), and **something
  everyone can keep**.


  The class writes it **together**, from the habits in this course: pause before
  you post, ask before sharing someone else, keep details for people you know,
  tell a trusted adult, and don't add to it when someone is having a hard time.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Should a class agreement be about what we do, or what we don't do?
    prompts:
      - "Which is easier to remember: 'We pause before we post' or 'Don't post
        mean things'?"
      - Which tells you what to do in the moment?
    notes: Positive lines say what to do. Both can work; a mix is fine if most are
      positive.
  activities:
    - at: make
      kind: activity
      title: Write our lines
      minutes: 10
      do: >
        In groups of three, write one or two lines for our agreement. Keep each
        under ten words if you can. Start with "We...".
      notes: Paper. Circulate and nudge don'ts into dos. No line names a real person
        or event.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Choose and agree
      minutes: 10
      do: >
        Groups read their lines. Put similar lines together. Choose about five
        that everyone can keep.
      notes: Read lines without naming groups. A thumbs up, sideways or down vote
        works; aim for lines everyone can keep.
    - at: end
      kind: info
      title: Where it lives
      do: >
        Our agreement will be kept where we can all see it. We'll look at it
        again in a few weeks.
      notes: Name the place (a poster, a page the school approves) and a date to
        revisit.
```
